claims.claim: Rooms/chambers were cut into the Externsteine rock: three chambers, stairways, an altar and a stone coffin cut into sandstone
claims.quote: The Grottenfels (I) contains a human-made "grotto" of three chambers connected by passages.

claims.claim: No document names the builders of these structures
claims.quote: However, it is unclear who could have built it here and why there is no written evidence of such a relatively elaborate undertaking.

claims.claim: The image in card 1 is a photochrom print of c.1890–1900, public domain
claims.quote:
Description: Externsteine in Germany.  Photochrom  print (color photo lithograph)
Date: between 1890 and 1900

claims.claim: A count built a fortress at the site that was not capable of defence
claims.quote: Circa 1660, Herman Adolph, Count of Lippe designed the area for use as a hunting lodge and Lustschloss. This was a fortress of two squat round towers flanking a central gatehouse, built against the eastern side of the Externsteine.

claims.claim: Excavated foundations show thin, ornamental walls
claims.quote: The excavated foundations show relatively thin walls, indicating that these walls were never intended as fortifications but were just ornamental.

claims.claim: The hunting lodge was torn down in 1810 at Countess Pauline's request
claims.quote: In 1810, it was torn down at the request of Countess Pauline.

claims.claim: The card 2 image is an engraving of 1663 by Elias van Lennep, public domain
claims.quote: Archive title: File:Externsteine Elias van Lennep 1663.png ... Author: Elias van Lennep  (Schulp); *1637/38, † 1692

claims.claim: The relief is the oldest monumental rock relief north of the Alps
claims.quote: Even assuming a high medieval date, the relief represents the oldest monumental relief worked into a natural rock face found north of the Alps.

claims.claim: Art historians formerly considered the relief Carolingian; since the 1950s it is dated to the 12th century, stylistically 1160 to 1170
claims.quote: formerly widely accepted as of Carolingian origin (9th century), scholarly consensus has placed it in the 12th century since the 1950s. From a stylistic point of view, historians today place the relief in the period 1160 to 1170.

claims.claim: The card 3 image is an 1862 drawing of the Externsteine relief, public domain
claims.quote:
Archive title: File:Externsteine Relief 1862.jpg
Description: Drawing of the Externsteine relief.
Date: 1862

claims.claim: In 1933 Heinrich Himmler became president of the Externsteine Foundation
claims.quote: In 1933, the "Externsteine Foundation" was established and Heinrich Himmler became its president.

claims.claim: The SS Ahnenerbe studied the stones
claims.quote: Interest in the location was furthered by the Ahnenerbe division within the SS, who studied the stones for their value to Germanic folklore and history.

claims.claim: An excavation in 1932 found no cultural remains
claims.quote: In 1932, the area was excavated (for the third time) by August Stieren but no "cultural remains" were discovered.

claims.claim: The card 4 image shows a carving on the Externsteine, photographed by Bär Minimum, CC0
claims.quote: Description: The letter W resembling the Wikipedia W engraved in the  w: Externsteine  rock formation in Germany ... Author: Bär Minimum  Licence: CC0

claims.claim: The carving photographed by Bär Minimum is modern
claims.quote: Description: The letter W resembling the Wikipedia W engraved in the  w: Externsteine  rock formation in Germany

claims.claim: Medieval builders cut the structures
claims.quote: Archaeological excavations at the site in the 1930s produced evidence for use from the late 10th to the 15th centuries.

claims.claim: The pagan-shrine story starts with one writer in 1564
claims.quote: The original claims associating the Externsteine with Saxon pagan worship were made by Hermann Hamelmann, who in his Delineatio Oppidorum Westfaliae (1564) claimed to take the information from older authorities

claims.claim: No finds support use of the site between the Stone Age and the 9th century
claims.quote: However, no archaeological evidence has been found that would substantiate use of the site between the end of the Upper Paleolithic and the Carolingian period (9th century).

claims.claim: The card 5 image shows the Externsteine in 2014, by 5snake5, CC0
claims.quote:
Description: Die Externsteine Sandstein-Formation im Teutoburger Wald, im Jahr 2014
Date: 2014-09-24 13:07:54
Author: 5snake5

claims.claim: Thirteen sandstone pillars stand in the Teutoburg Forest near Horn-Bad Meinberg
claims.quote: It terminates in a series of 13 highly visible and mostly free-standing pillars.

claims.claim: Rock II rises 37.5 m
claims.quote: The next one, II, is also known as Turmfels (tower) and rises 37.5 m (123 ft) above the surrounding area.

claims.claim: Rock II is the tallest of the pillars
claims.quote: The largest is rock I (subdivided into Ia and Ib), also known as the Grottenfels due to its cave.

claims.claim: There is a high chamber with an altar and a circular window
claims.quote: At the east of the Höhenkammer is an apse with a circular window and an altar.

claims.claim: There is an open stone sarcophagus in an arched alcove
claims.quote: An arched alcove with an open stone sarcophagus at the bottom has been cut into the sandstone.

claims.claim: A platform was cut on top of the rock
claims.quote: The top of rock Ia has been turned into a platform and is reached by a stone stairway that begins between rocks I and II.

claims.claim: An inscription in the main chamber records an altar consecrated in 1115
claims.quote: In the main chamber is an inscription dated to 1115, indicating that an altar was consecrated here.

claims.claim: The Descent from the Cross relief is on the outside of the rock
claims.quote: The outside of rock I also features the Kreuzabnahmerelief (showing Christ's Descent from the Cross).

claims.claim: Hamelmann wrote in 1564 that Charlemagne made an altar from the "rock of the magpies", then a pagan idol
claims.quote: "Horn is famous for the "rock of the magpies", an ancient monument mentioned by older writers. I have read that Charlemagne from this rock of the magpies, then a pagan idol, made a consecrated altar decorated with images of the apostles."

claims.claim: A 19th-century local historian tied that idol to the Saxon Irminsul
claims.quote: Local amateur historian Gotthilf August Benjamin Schierenberg (1808–1894) seems to have been the first to identify the "pagan idol" mentioned by Hamelmann with the Saxon Irminsul.

claims.claim: Wilhelm Teudt called the stones the "Germanic Stonehenge"
claims.quote: Since the mid-1920s he had popularized them by calling them the "Germanic Stonehenge".

claims.claim: Excavations found stone tools of the Ahrensburg culture, roughly 10,700–9,600 BC, and medieval material
claims.quote: Attribution of objects found was either to the Mesolithic Ahrensburg culture (see above) or to the medieval period

claims.claim: Bronze and Iron Age finds were conspicuously absent
claims.quote: with evidence of occupation in the Bronze or Iron Age conspicuously absent

claims.claim: One suggestion is that the site was a copy of the Holy Sepulchre for pilgrims unable to reach Jerusalem
claims.quote: The remains visible today indicate the possibility that the Externsteine were intended as a destination for pilgrims unable to travel to Jerusalem.

claims.claim: The 2014 photograph shows the path at the site
claims.quote: pathtoday.jpg shows a broad gravel path leading between the rock pillars, with walkers, benches and a dog; archive record: "Die Externsteine Sandstein-Formation im Teutoburger Wald, im Jahr 2014"
